summary:
No Rize-specific measure, enforcement programme or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sourced material: what a trans visitor faces in the province is the national framework of Turkey, which Rize stands under in full.

That framework has been moving toward criminalisation without the prohibitions yet being on the books. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Reform package would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people, describing it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against its LGBT provisions. Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain, none of which were ultimately submitted to parliament.

The provisions were removed from the packages brought forward in 2026, and a February 2026 press report of a proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package. The absence of the statute has not removed street-level exposure: foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention, and every stop is an occasion on which documents are read against presentation.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender change has been available since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Pride events are the most heavily policed flashpoint. Authorities have banned Pride in Istanbul and most other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against those who defied the bans. In June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at the end of the year.

Transition-related care is tightening. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency, within the Ministry of Health, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.

Organisational space is also contracting. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images on social media incompatible with "society's moral values" and that it could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities.
tangentialFactors:
The pending nature of the draft packages is itself a live risk factor: three separate packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 without being tabled, and the February 2026 proposal on public encouragement of conduct "contrary to biological sex" circulated as a press report rather than an enacted measure. Enforcement rhetoric and administrative action have repeatedly run ahead of statute.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service in Turkey. Conscripts who declare homosexuality are assessed under a definition treating it as a "psychosexual illness", must supply photographic proof, and risk an "unfit report" leaking publicly, which is a documented outing channel relevant to any trans or gender-nonconforming man of conscription age.

The documented pattern of detention is asymmetric in its handling of victims. Rights reporting cited within the national framework describes a trans woman knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul in August 2024 whose attacker was released while she herself was referred for arrest, and six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings.

The 2025 national report cited in the national framework counted 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, of which 43 were taken off the record.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available in Turkey since 1988, but the draft packages made public in 2025 would have made it nearly impossible to obtain, and no resident can treat the current procedure as settled.

No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity exists at national level, so residents have no general statutory complaint to file after being refused service, housing or employment.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and recognition of a partner's status does not follow from a gender change.

The İzmir court's December 2025 dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association sets a direct precedent for resident organisations: registering, collecting donations and posting to social media all carry dissolution risk on "moral values" grounds.

Access to hormone therapy is restricted for people under 21 by the June 2025 Ministry of Health agency ban, which constrains transition timelines for younger residents.

LGBT detainees in Turkish prisons are held by registered sex in gendered facilities, with arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement, restricted healthcare and complaints procedures that are ineffective and can invite further violence.
